content.thinking:
Since whimsical doesn't call for a specific kit, I'll skip it and just use paint plus cards for the style. Now I'm sketching the capybara's proportions, starting from its real-world size and scaling up into a chunky, exaggerated whimsical form.

I'm working out the skeleton layout—placing hips at the root, running a spine chain from rump to chest, then a short neck into a blunt, boxy head with a down-sloped snout, plus a tiny tail nub since capybaras barely have a visible tail.

For the limbs I'm planning front legs with shoulder-elbow-wrist-paw joints and rear legs similarly, giving front paws four toes and rear paws three. Rather than jointing every toe individually I'll keep toes as single-joint stub capsules per digit to stay within budget, with small dark cone nails, and finally I'm adding a small whimsical bird perched on the capybara's head as a round little accent piece.

Skipping the yuzu idea, but maybe a tiny daisy tucked behind the ear works nicely alongside the blush. No ground needed, just the animal itself, though I'm tempted to add a small blade of grass hanging from the capybara's mouth for charm, even with the separate jaw pieces in rest pose.

Now I'm planning the fur texture with scattered tufts across a warm ginger-brown coat, cream belly, and darker snout, using countershading and grain for streaks, then roughing out the whimsical proportions: a big round barrel body, blocky rounded head, and oversized bulging nose.

For the face, I'm thinking small eyes placed high on the sides, tiny rounded ears, and cheerful cartoon eyes built from a dark sphere plus a tiny white highlight sphere, with small brow arcs to give a friendly, contented expression. I'm settling on real-world scale proportions, roughly 1 to 1.3 meters long and 0.5 to 0.6 meters at the shoulder, and starting to lay out body coordinates from the rump backward.

Working out the precise coordinates for the body ellipse, spine height, short legs, and head placement, including nose tip position and skull height, then setting up the spine joint chain for rigging...

Still defining the skeleton hierarchy...

Defining joint hierarchy...

Adding more body stations...

Capping body at z≈0.4 gives total length about 1.2m with shoulder height around 0.6, matching real capybara proportions well. Now I'm working out leg placement — front legs sweeping down from the shoulders, hind legs from the hips, keeping them short and thick-tapered to match the animal's stocky build.

I'll use a 3-segment hind leg with knee bent forward and hock back, ending at the foot target. For paws, I'm making flattened ellipsoid pads with 4 toes on front feet and 3 on rear, each toe a short forward-extending capsule with a small nail cone, giving them a chubby, whimsical look.

I should check that legs stay mostly visible beyond the body silhouette given the root positions, and add some hammy bulge to the rear thighs for a chunkier look. For fur, I'm thinking of layering a countershaded, mottled pattern with grain streaks and maybe a subtly darker stripe running along the back to mimic capybara coloring.

For fur tufts, I'm planning to render them as small tapered-strand card textures tinted by the paint at each card's root, scattering roughly 450 cards across the body (plus fewer on legs and cheeks) with a minimum spacing of about 0.035 to keep them from overlapping, using simple low-poly geometry per card to keep the triangle count down.

Now I'm shaping the head as a lofted sweep of stations from the back of the skull to the nose, blocking out width and height at each cross-section — but I'm realizing a literal real-capybara proportion makes the head too long (about 0.5m), so I'm scaling it back to a shorter, chunkier whimsical head instead.

I'm splitting the jaw into two pieces: the cranium/upper jaw as one loft along the head bone, and a separate small lower jaw block tucked underneath on its own bone, positioning the mouth line so the muzzle mostly hides the lower jaw.

I want to add a dark smile-line decal sweeping along the cheeks to hide the seam between the separate head parts, then add a rounded dark brownish-pink nose pad with two small nostril spheres on top of the snout. For the eyes, I'm placing them high on the sides of the head with a bit of gloss for a whimsical look.

Now I'm working out the ears—small rounded ellipsoid shapes near the back top of the head, outer shell scaled flatter with a smaller pink inner piece, rigged with hinge joints for animation. I'm also placing a small chubby round bird standing between the ears on top of the head, sized about 10cm with a tiny tail, figuring out its exact position relative to the head's loft geometry.

I'm designing the bird as a cute bluebird-ish character: sky blue back, cream belly, orange beak, maybe a tiny yellow crest. I'm planning its skeleton with a bird-prefixed naming scheme—root, head, upper and lower beak (jaw role), two-joint wing chains, a two-joint tail chain, and leg chains with simple toe parts—oriented facing forward but angled slightly to look outward.

For the body shape, I'm sizing the ellipsoid and considering using a scaled sphere part painted with a countershade (blue over cream) since that relies on surface normals rather than UV coordinates, so it works fine with primitive spheres rather than needing a lofted mesh.

Now I'm detailing the head: a small sphere for the skull, an orange cone beak with a tinier lower mandible, black bead eyes with a white highlight spark, folded leaf-shaped wings in blue with darker tips jointed at the shoulder, a fanned three-feather tail, a tiny head crest, and thin orange legs with three forward toes — keeping accessories minimal rather than adding a hat or flower. I also want to check that the bird's feet land cleanly on top of the capybara's head without clipping, using the gap preview, and I'm thinking about adding a whimsical blush decal on the capybara's cheeks via a painted sphere pattern.

For the blush, I'll use a flat pale pink-orange oval decal rather than a gradient cutout, plus tiny freckle dots on the nose, a few curved dark whisker sweeps on each side of the muzzle with paler whisker pad bumps, and small brow tufts. I also want to add subtle hints of teeth — small cream rounded boxes peeking just under the closed upper lip and lower jaw, instead of the big orange incisors a real capybara would show.

Now I'm adding whimsical touches: a thin green grass blade sweeping out from the mouth's corner along the jaw, and a tiny daisy tucked near the left ear with a yellow center and a ring of six petals. I'm also keeping track of the palette to stay within 64 colors, covering fur, belly, nose, dark accents, pink, cream, tooth, blue tones, orange, yellow, green, and white.

Still writing fur details...

Still blending coat colors...

Now I'm setting up side mirroring conventions, using world coordinates where positive X is the left side, and starting the capybara builder with its paint canvas size.

I'm deciding on texture resolution by calculating grain size against texel density, settling on 1024 as fine enough for the fur detail. Then I'm laying out the skeleton, starting with the hips as the root joint and building the spine chain along a curved path from pelvis through the torso.

I continue the chain into the neck with two more joints curving upward, then place the head joint at the neck's tip, working out where it should attach and aim.

Adding more joints...

For rear legs with 3 segments (thigh, shin, foot), the vertical reach is substantial relative to segment lengths, so I'm bending the hock backward and forward appropriately, naming the chain hipL/kneeL/hockL/footL with the last name as the tip. For front legs with 2 segments, the tip becomes "pawL" following the same spans+1 naming convention.

The leg roots parent off the hips for rear and spine joint for front, and I'm sweeping each chain into a smooth tapered tube with tip radii like [0.08,0.05] for front and a thicker [0.1,0.055] for the hind thigh, adding a small sphere for the paw at each tip.

Fur gets slightly darker toward the feet using a y-based gradient from coat color to a darker brown. Then I'm placing toe joints on each paw tip (4 for front, 3 for rear), positioning each one forward and outward from the paw center with a forward aim direction.

Still building toe geometry...

I realize the round cap would push the nose tip too far forward, making the head disproportionately long, so I'm reconsidering a blunter muzzle shape—using flat end caps instead, with a separate nose pad sculpted as a scaled sphere, to keep the capybara's head compact and rounder.

Placing the ears at the back of the head and the little bird perched on top near the front, I'm deciding on sweep smoothness—using 10-12 sides for a soft, slightly faceted whimsical look rather than a perfect circle. For the snout tip around (0,.40,.745), I'm planning a dark nose pad sphere and cheek fur details to round out the capybara's face.

Adjusting the blush decal direction and size, and deciding to use opaque pale colors instead of semi-transparent ones to avoid alpha-composite darkening issues. Then placing the dark eye spheres symmetrically based on the head's width at that z-position.

Working out eye placement with surface sticking...

For personality, I'm adding eyelids and a brow tuft -- a small dark capsule above the eye plus a sleepy half-lid dome over the top third of the eye, using a clipped hemisphere in the fur color to give that serene capybara look.

I'll offset the lid sphere up and outward from the eye center so it covers the top portion, giving a sleepy, content look that pairs nicely with the bird perched on its head. For the ears, I'm going with small rounded capybara-style ears, slightly whimsical and larger, using a scaled sphere shape.

Each ear gets an outer furred part and a smaller pink inner piece on the forward-facing side, hinged at joints near the head. I'm adding whiskers as thin curved sweeps from the snout, and now thinking through the mouth line to keep that same gentle capybara expression.

For the mouth, I'm draping a thin dark path along the muzzle's lower edge rather than trying to carve a separate seam, and considering building the lower jaw as its own lofted piece along the jaw bone so it naturally sits under the muzzle and creates the mouth opening visually.

I'm placing the jaw lower and narrower than the head so it peeks out as a visible chin a few centimeters below, which should read as cute, and I'm weighing whether to add extra dark lip-line sweeps or just rely on whisker pad bumps and a simple smile decal on the head's side.

I'm sizing and positioning tiny cream incisor boxes hanging just below the front of the muzzle, hiding the lower set under the jaw, and planning to double-check exact placement against a preview since the muzzle's curved bottom edge makes the math tricky. I'm also sketching a grass blade path starting from the mouth corner at the jaw-line.

Writing blade outline shape...

Writing fur strand paths...

Still working out bird geometry...

Still working out wing geometry...

Switching to tapered frustum boxes for the tail feathers instead, fanning three quills with a slight splay and color variation, then moving on to defining the bird skeleton joints—root, head, beak, and jaw.

Now I'm wiring up wing joints under the root, a single tail joint aimed backward, and leg chains for each side using a hip-to-foot naming scheme so the tips resolve correctly. All joints nest under the head root, which should keep things consistent, and next I'm placing a ring of petal spheres near the right ear to form a daisy decoration.

Trying spike-shaped petals arranged radially outward from a center point...

I'm thinking fur cards might cover the daisy so I'll add it after the cards, and skipping extra body details like belly folds since the fur and paint handle most texture. For the skeleton, I'm working out the bone chain order—tail, hips, spine—making sure the body path and chest cap stay within the last bone's range without needing a separate neck bone.

Now I'm figuring out the neck sweep as a thicker chain from z .3 to .46, tapering from radius .19 to .17 with an elliptical cross-section so it blends into the head start, keeping it the same coat color as the body. I'm also checking that the head joint parents off the end of the neck chain so the head rotates correctly around that pivot, and confirming the hips root sits centered at x=0 with the spine's first joint properly linked as a child of hips.

For the paints, I'm building the coat with a countershading function for the body and a mottled pattern for the belly using two tan tones, making sure the card tint reads from the coat including the belly region, and darkening the toe nails. I'm setting up the fur scatter on the body sweep with a density and minimum distance filter that excludes the underside, then sizing the fur cards appropriately.

For the head, I need to restrict scatter to the cheeks and avoid the muzzle and eye regions, so I'm adding a filter based on z-position and distance checks around the eye points to keep cards out of those areas, while cards render double-sided along the surface frame normals. Head cards get a smaller size range, and I'm scattering fur on the upper legs as well with their own density.

Now I'm working out the helper function and coordinates for building limbs, treating returned points as a polyline path for the chain, and figuring out eye placement on the head surface using azimuth and elevation angles to compute a direction vector from the head center.

Since I'm unsure how the embed offset actually translates geometry-origin-to-surface, I'll just place eye and lid spheres explicitly using the hit point and normal—nudging the eye slightly outside the surface and the lid just above and in front of it—then verify visually once rendered.

I'm also planning a small tapered brow capsule above the eyelid, angled upward toward the outer edge for a cute effect, to add later once the main geometry is in place. Now I'm sketching out an SVG fur-tuft texture using layered curved paths to mimic wisps of hair.

For the bird, I'm deciding to skip feather cards and build the crest from spikes instead, and sketching the body coloring as a cheerful bluebird with blue back, orange-russet chest, and cream belly via a countershading gradient paint function.

input.command: sed -n 1,40p src/ik.ts; grep -n "soft\|level" src/paint.ts | head; grep -n "keepOut" src/surface.ts | head -5
